services/issue/milestone_burndown.go
// Copyright 2026 The Gitea Authors. All rights reserved.
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT

package issue

import (
	"cmp"
	"context"
	"math"
	"slices"
	"time"

	issues_model "gitea.dev/models/issues"
	"gitea.dev/modules/setting"
	"gitea.dev/modules/timeutil"
)

// BurndownStatus says what the chart can tell about when a milestone will finish.
type BurndownStatus string

const (
	BurndownEmpty            BurndownStatus = "empty"             // nothing has ever been in the milestone
	BurndownDone             BurndownStatus = "done"              // every item in it is closed
	BurndownClosed           BurndownStatus = "closed"            // the milestone was closed with items still open
	BurndownProjected        BurndownStatus = "projected"         // a finish date could be extrapolated
	BurndownNotBurning       BurndownStatus = "not_burning"       // remaining work has not fallen over the window
	BurndownInsufficientData BurndownStatus = "insufficient_data" // too few days of history to extrapolate
)

const (
	burndownWindowDays     = 14  // the projection extrapolates the net burn rate over at most this many days
	burndownMinHistoryDays = 2   // a rate over fewer days is noise, not a trend
	burndownHorizonDays    = 365 // a due date further out than this past the chart is not drawn
)

// BurndownPoint is the state of a milestone at the end of one day.
type BurndownPoint struct {
	Date      string `json:"date"`      // "YYYY-MM-DD" in the instance zone, so every viewer sees the same day
	Remaining int    `json:"remaining"` // items in the milestone and open
	Scope     int    `json:"scope"`     // items in the milestone, open or closed
	Added     int    `json:"added"`     // items that joined the milestone this day, after its first day of work
	Removed   int    `json:"removed"`   // items that left the milestone this day, after its first day of work

	Changes []BurndownChange `json:"changes,omitempty"` // what moved the counts this day, in order; omitted on quiet days
}

// BurndownChangeKind is how one item changed the milestone's counts.
type BurndownChangeKind string

const (
	BurndownChangeClosed   BurndownChangeKind = "closed" // a merge counts as a close
	BurndownChangeReopened BurndownChangeKind = "reopened"
	BurndownChangeAdded    BurndownChangeKind = "added"
	BurndownChangeRemoved  BurndownChangeKind = "removed"
)

// BurndownChange is one item that changed the milestone's counts on a day.
type BurndownChange struct {
	Index  int64              `json:"index"`
	Title  string             `json:"title"`
	IsPull bool               `json:"isPull"`
	Kind   BurndownChangeKind `json:"kind"`
}

// BurndownOptions says which kinds of item to count. A caller must leave out any kind the viewer cannot read.
type BurndownOptions struct {
	Issues bool
	Pulls  bool
}

// BurndownIdeal is the straight line from the first day with work to zero on the due date.
type BurndownIdeal struct {
	From      string `json:"from"`
	FromValue int    `json:"fromValue"`
	To        string `json:"to"` // the due date; the line always ends at zero
}

// MilestoneBurndown is everything the milestone page charts.
type MilestoneBurndown struct {
	Points      []BurndownPoint `json:"points"`
	Deadline    string          `json:"deadline"` // empty when there is no due date, or it is too far out to draw
	Ideal       *BurndownIdeal  `json:"ideal"`
	Status      BurndownStatus  `json:"status"`
	Projected   string          `json:"projected"`   // set only when Status is projected
	DaysLate    *int            `json:"daysLate"`    // projected finish minus the due date; negative is early
	CompletedOn string          `json:"completedOn"` // set only when Status is done
}

type burndownState struct {
	inScope bool
	open    bool
}

type burndownDelta struct {
	at        int64
	remaining int
	scope     int
	item      *issues_model.MilestoneItem
}

func (d burndownDelta) moves() bool {
	return d.remaining != 0 || d.scope != 0
}

// kind names the change for the day's list; a change of scope outranks a close, since an item that
// joins already closed was added, not closed. It is empty when the counts did not move.
func (d burndownDelta) kind() BurndownChangeKind {
	switch {
	case d.scope > 0:
		return BurndownChangeAdded
	case d.scope < 0:
		return BurndownChangeRemoved
	case d.remaining < 0:
		return BurndownChangeClosed
	case d.remaining > 0:
		return BurndownChangeReopened
	}
	return ""
}

func (s burndownState) counts() (remaining, scope int) {
	if s.inScope {
		scope = 1
		if s.open {
			remaining = 1
		}
	}
	return remaining, scope
}

// diff is the change in the milestone's counts when an item moves from s to next
func (s burndownState) diff(next burndownState, at int64) burndownDelta {
	r0, s0 := s.counts()
	r1, s1 := next.counts()
	return burndownDelta{at: at, remaining: r1 - r0, scope: s1 - s0}
}

// replayMilestoneItem turns one item's comments into changes to the milestone's counts. Missing history
// is filled in so the replay always ends where the database is now: an item in the milestone with no
// comment saying it joined (migrated issues have none) joins when it was created or the milestone was,
// and a closed item with no close comment closes at its closed_unix.
func replayMilestoneItem(item issues_model.MilestoneItem, events []issues_model.MilestoneEvent, milestoneID, milestoneCreated int64) []burndownDelta {
	events = slices.Clone(events) // synthetic events are appended below
	created := int64(item.CreatedUnix)
	var firstScope *issues_model.MilestoneEvent
	hasClose := false
	for i := range events {
		switch events[i].Type {
		case issues_model.CommentTypeMilestone:
			if firstScope == nil {
				firstScope = &events[i]
			}
		case issues_model.CommentTypeClose, issues_model.CommentTypeMergePull:
			hasClose = true
		}
	}

	// synthetic events take id 0 so they sort before a real comment in the same second
	joinAt := max(created, milestoneCreated)
	if firstScope == nil && item.MilestoneID == milestoneID {
		events = append(events, issues_model.MilestoneEvent{Type: issues_model.CommentTypeMilestone, MilestoneID: milestoneID, CreatedUnix: timeutil.TimeStamp(joinAt)})
	} else if firstScope != nil && firstScope.MilestoneID != milestoneID {
		// its first recorded move is out of the milestone, so it was in it before then
		joinAt = min(joinAt, int64(firstScope.CreatedUnix))
		events = append(events, issues_model.MilestoneEvent{Type: issues_model.CommentTypeMilestone, MilestoneID: milestoneID, CreatedUnix: timeutil.TimeStamp(joinAt)})
	}
	if item.IsClosed && !hasClose {
		// a close time of zero predates the item, so clamp it as the Activity issues chart does
		closedAt := max(int64(item.ClosedUnix), created)
		events = append(events, issues_model.MilestoneEvent{Type: issues_model.CommentTypeClose, CreatedUnix: timeutil.TimeStamp(closedAt)})
	}
	slices.SortFunc(events, issues_model.CompareMilestoneEvents)

	state := burndownState{open: true}
	lastAt := created
	deltas := make([]burndownDelta, 0, len(events)+1)
	for _, e := range events {
		next := state
		switch e.Type {
		case issues_model.CommentTypeMilestone:
			if e.MilestoneID == milestoneID {
				next.inScope = true
			} else if e.OldMilestoneID == milestoneID {
				next.inScope = false
			}
		case issues_model.CommentTypeClose, issues_model.CommentTypeMergePull:
			next.open = false
		case issues_model.CommentTypeReopen:
			next.open = true
		}
		// a close or reopen while the item is outside the milestone moves no count; recording it would
		// stretch a closed milestone's chart to a change that never touched it
		if d := state.diff(next, int64(e.CreatedUnix)); d.moves() {
			deltas = append(deltas, d)
			lastAt = max(lastAt, d.at)
		}
		state = next
	}

	// the comments can still disagree with the row, for instance after a reopen whose close was never

## Summary
A Gitea milestone page shows only a progress bar and the current open and closed counts. There's no way to see how work progressed over the milestone's life, whether the team is on track for the due date, or when scope was added mid-way.

This feature adds a **burndown chart** to the milestone page. It compares the open items left each day against an **ideal line**, marks scope changes, and projects a **finish date** from the current pace. It helps teams running sprints or releases (like our own course sprints) spot a slipping milestone early, and helps leads explain *why*, for example because issues were added partway through.

## User Story
As a team lead, I want a burndown chart for each milestone comparing actual progress against an ideal pace so that I can tell early whether we'll finish by the due date and see when scope changed.

## User Scenario
A team lead opens their sprint milestone at `/{owner}/{repo}/milestone/{id}` a week before its due date. Above the issue list is a chart titled "Burndown" with a one-line summary: "Projected to finish on Oct 21, 2 days after the due date".
- The remaining line sits above the dashed ideal line from day 3 onwards. A ▲ on day 3 shows that two items were added to the milestone that day.
- Hovering day 3 lists them, "Added to milestone: #9 Support SSO" and "#10 Audit log", and the same list appears under the chart with links.
- The lead ticks "Include pull requests" to count the sprint's pull requests too, and the page URL gains `include_pulls=1`. They paste that URL into the team chat, and teammates who open it see the same chart.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] AC1: Given a milestone with items, when its page loads, then a chart shows the open items left at the end of each day as the **actual** line, and a straight **ideal** line from the first day with work down to zero on the due date.
- [ ] AC2: Given items that were closed and reopened, or moved between milestones, when the chart is drawn, then each past day's counts reflect the timeline events (milestone changes, closes, merges, reopens), and the last day matches the milestone's progress bar.
- [ ] AC3: Given items added to or removed from the milestone after its first day of work, then the chart marks those days (▲ added, ▼ removed).
- [ ] AC4: Given at least two days of history since work began and a falling count, then a projected finish date is drawn and stated, compared with the due date. With too little history, no burn-down, all work done, or a closed milestone, the projection is hidden and the summary says why.
- [ ] AC5: Given a day on which items changed, when the user hovers that day, then the items that changed are listed (closed, reopened, added, removed). The same list appears under the chart with links, because a chart tooltip can't hold links.
- [ ] AC6: Given the "Include pull requests" checkbox, then it is off by default, ticking it counts pull requests too, and its state is kept in the page URL (`include_pulls=1`) without changing the issue list's own filters.
- [ ] AC7: The edge cases behave as follows:
  - **No due date:** no ideal line, with a note saying why. A projected date is still shown.
  - **Due date changed:** the current due date is used.
  - **Overdue:** the chart runs to today.
  - **Closed milestone:** the chart ends at its close date.
  - **Item added after it was already closed:** the total rises but the open count doesn't.
  - **Empty milestone:** an empty-state message instead of a chart.
- [ ] AC8: Given a viewer who can't read the milestone's issues or pull requests, then neither the chart nor its data endpoint reveals them. A viewer who can read only one kind sees only that kind, and a reader of pull requests only sees pull requests by default.
- [ ] AC9: All new UI strings are in `options/locale/locale_en-US.json`.
- [ ] AC10: Unit tests cover the timeline replay (close/reopen, add, remove and move between milestones, add-after-closed), the ideal line and the projection. Integration tests cover the pull request toggle and the permission rules.

## Out of Scope
- An `/api/v1` endpoint for the burndown data.
- Story points or weights. Gitea has none, so every item counts as one.
- Burndown charts on the milestones list or on the user dashboard.
- A per-viewer time zone. Days follow the instance's time zone, the one due dates are stored in.
- History of issues later transferred to another repository: they drop out of every past day, because history is read for the milestone's own repository.

## Open Questions
None. Resolved during implementation:
- With no due date, the projected finish date is still shown, though the original spec said to hide it, because a finish date is useful without a deadline. Only the ideal line is hidden.
- A projection more than a year past the chart is stated in the summary but not drawn, so it can't squash the history.

## Design Decision
**Decision:** Rebuild each milestone's history when the chart is requested, by replaying its items' timeline comments (milestone changes, closes, merges and reopens), and serve it from a separate JSON endpoint that the page loads after it renders.

**Alternatives Considered:**
- A daily snapshot table filled by a scheduled job, which the chart reads directly.
- Deriving the chart from each issue's current `created_unix` and `closed_unix`, as the Activity tab's issues chart (#13) does.

**Rationale:** Snapshots need a migration and a new scheduled job, and they only start recording on the day they ship, so every existing milestone would have no history. Current timestamps can't show an issue that was reopened, or one that moved between milestones, which AC2 requires. Replaying comments works for every existing milestone straight away, needs no schema change, and is exact for anything Gitea recorded.

**Consequences:**
- The milestone columns on `comment` aren't indexed and `comment` has no `repo_id`. The query is bounded by the indexed comment type and a join on the repository's issues, and runs on its own lazy request so it can't slow the issue list.
- Issues migrated from other platforms have no milestone comments. The replay falls back to each issue's row and always ends on the database's current state, so the chart agrees with the progress bar.
- The milestone pages admit readers of issues *or* pull requests, so the endpoint filters by kind for each viewer (AC8).

### Further decisions made during implementation
- **Count issues by default, pull requests on request (AC6).** Alternative: always count both, as the progress bar does. The issue asked for a toggle defaulting to issues, and per-kind permission filtering makes either default safe.

```sh
#!/bin/bash
# Seeds a demo repo + sprint milestone through the API, then backdates the timeline so the burndown has history.
set -euo pipefail
B=http://localhost:3001/api/v1
U=burndown-demo P='Burndown-demo-2026'
DB=/Users/asb/WM/SWE/gitea/data/gitea.db
api() { curl -sf -u "$U:$P" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -X "$1" "$B$2" ${3:+-d "$3"}; }

api POST /user/repos '{"name":"sprint-demo","auto_init":true,"default_branch":"main"}' >/dev/null
R=/repos/$U/sprint-demo
DUE=$(date -u -v+5d +%Y-%m-%dT23:59:59Z)
MS=$(api POST $R/milestones "{\"title\":\"Sprint 2\",\"description\":\"Course sprint\",\"due_on\":\"$DUE\"}" | python3 -c 'import sys,json;print(json.load(sys.stdin)["id"])')

titles=("Login page layout" "Password reset email" "Profile settings form" "Avatar upload" "Notification badges"
  "Search results paging" "Dark mode toggle" "Keyboard shortcuts" "Support SSO" "Audit log")
for i in "${!titles[@]}"; do
  n=$((i+1))
  if [ $n -le 8 ]; then
    api POST $R/issues "{\"title\":\"${titles[$i]}\",\"milestone\":$MS}" >/dev/null
  else
    api POST $R/issues "{\"title\":\"${titles[$i]}\"}" >/dev/null
    api PATCH $R/issues/$n "{\"milestone\":$MS}" >/dev/null  # writes a milestone comment, so it shows as added
  fi
done
# one PR in the milestone for the "Include pull requests" toggle
api POST $R/contents/feature.txt '{"content":"ZmVhdHVyZQo=","message":"add feature","new_branch":"feature"}' >/dev/null
api POST $R/pulls "{\"title\":\"Implement login page\",\"head\":\"feature\",\"base\":\"main\",\"milestone\":$MS}" >/dev/null

close() { api PATCH $R/issues/$1 '{"state":"closed"}' >/dev/null; }
reopen() { api PATCH $R/issues/$1 '{"state":"open"}' >/dev/null; }
for n in 1 2 3 4 5 9; do close $n; done
reopen 3; close 3; reopen 9

# backdate: day offsets relative to today (negative = days ago); one row per event
RID=$(sqlite3 $DB "select id from repository where name='sprint-demo'")
d() { echo $(( $(date +%s) + $1*86400 )); }
sqlite3 $DB <<SQL
update milestone set created_unix=$(d -10) where id=$MS;
update issue set created_unix=$(d -10) where repo_id=$RID and "index"<=8;
update issue set created_unix=$(d -7) where repo_id=$RID and "index" in (9,10);
update issue set created_unix=$(d -9) where repo_id=$RID and "index"=11;
update comment set created_unix=(select created_unix from issue where id=comment.issue_id)
  where issue_id in (select id from issue where repo_id=$RID) and type=8;
SQL
# closes/reopens in creation order: 1,2,3,4,5,9 closed; 3 reopened then closed again; 9 reopened
mapfile -t ids < <(sqlite3 $DB "select c.id from comment c join issue i on i.id=c.issue_id where i.repo_id=$RID and c.type in (1,2) order by c.id")
days=(-9 -8 -8 -6 -4 -3 -5 -2 -1)
for k in "${!ids[@]}"; do
  sqlite3 $DB "update comment set created_unix=$(d ${days[$k]}) where id=${ids[$k]}"
done
sqlite3 $DB "update issue set closed_unix=(select max(created_unix) from comment where issue_id=issue.id and type=2) where repo_id=$RID and is_closed=1"
echo "http://localhost:3001/$U/sprint-demo/milestone/$MS"

```

# Section 3: SE Process: One Issue's Full Lifecycle (2.5 min)

This section has two parts.

## Part A: Backlog Composition

Describe how your team built the Sprint 1 backlog. Cover:

1. **Estimation strategy**: how did you estimate issues? Story points, planning poker, or another method? Who participated in the estimation: the whole team, just the assignee, or a subset?
2. **Prioritization strategy**: what drove the order of issues in the backlog and what drove the selection of issues for the sprint?
3. **What you'd do differently**: what was hard or unclear in this process, and what 1–2 specific changes will you make to how you compose the Sprint 2 backlog?

Keep this part brief: the goal is to establish whether the team used a deliberate process, not to walk through every issue.

## Part B: One Illustrative Issue

Pick the **one issue** from Sprint **1** that best represents your team's SE practices. Try to select one that was interesting and significant. Walk through its complete lifecycle:

**The issue itself**: show the issue, then describe briefly (do not read it verbatim):
* User story or scenario
* Key acceptance criteria
* Key open questions and out-of-scope points

**Estimation**: what was the estimated effort, and what was the actual effort roughly? Explain if the estimation was accurate and why it was or it was not accurate (e.g. what aspects or possible scenarios did you miss in your estimation?).

**Analysis and design**: how did you figure out where in the codebase to make the change (concept location)? What was the expected impact on other parts of the system (impact analysis)? Was this a small or large change? Briefly describe the design of your solution before implementation began. If an AI agent/tool assisted, how did you verify its output?

**Implementation**: was there back-and-forth with the AI agent/tool to get the implementation right? Why? Summarize the scope of the change: roughly how many files, what types of files, and how many lines were changed. Show the resulting feature through UI screenshots or a short video clip; no code screenshots.

**Quality checks**: how did you test this issue, and what did the code review surface? For testing: what tests were designed and written and how did you verify the tests were correct? Don't enumerate tests, give a broad description/categorization or give interesting examples. For review: what was the strategy, were any problems found, and how were they resolved?

**Reflection**: Did the team apply this level of rigor to all Sprint 1 issues? If not, what was skipped and why? This is expected: teams make tradeoffs. The reflection shows you understand where you cut corners, the cost, and how to improve your process.----
## Design Decision
**Decision:** Rebuild each milestone's history when the chart is requested, by replaying its items' timeline comments (milestone changes, closes, merges and reopens), and serve it from a separate JSON endpoint that the page loads after it renders.

**Alternatives Considered:**
- A daily snapshot table filled by a scheduled job, which the chart reads directly.
- Deriving the chart from each issue's current `created_unix` and `closed_unix`, as the Activity tab's issues chart (#13) does.

**Rationale:** Snapshots need a migration and a new scheduled job, and they only start recording on the day they ship, so every existing milestone would have no history. Current timestamps can't show an issue that was reopened, or one that moved between milestones, which the acceptance criteria require. Replaying comments works for every existing milestone straight away, needs no schema change, and is exact for anything Gitea recorded.

**Consequences:**
- The milestone columns on `comment` aren't indexed and `comment` has no `repo_id`. The query is bounded by the indexed comment type and a join on the repository's issues, and runs on its own lazy request so it can't slow the issue list.
- Issues migrated from other platforms have no milestone comments. The replay falls back to each issue's row and always ends on the database's current state, so the chart agrees with the progress bar.
- Dates are bucketed in the server's time zone, the zone due dates are stored in, so every viewer sees the same days.
- The milestone pages admit readers of issues *or* pull requests, so the endpoint has to filter by kind for each viewer. It does, and this is tested.

Closes #14

## What changed

The milestone page (`/{owner}/{repo}/milestone/{id}`) now has a burndown chart above the issue list, folded under a "Burndown" heading that collapses. It shows:

- **Remaining:** open items at the end of each day, stepping on the day each change happened.
- **Total in milestone:** a dashed line with ▲ where items were added and ▼ where they were removed. The milestone's first day of work is its plan, so it is not marked.
- **Ideal:** a straight line from the first day with work down to zero on the due date.
- **Projected finish:** a dotted line extrapolated from the net burn rate over the last 14 days. A one-line summary says in words whether that is early, on the due date or late, or why there is no projection yet.
- **Hover details:** hovering a day lists the items that changed on it (closed, reopened, added, removed; a merge counts as closed). The same list appears under the chart with a link to each item, since links can't be clicked inside a canvas tooltip. It starts on the latest day with changes.
- **Include pull requests:** a checkbox, off by default, kept in the page URL as `include_pulls=1` without disturbing the issue list's own filters.

History is rebuilt from timeline comments (milestone changes, closes, merges and reopens), not from the current state. There is no schema change and no migration. The chart loads from its own endpoint, `GET /{owner}/{repo}/milestone/{id}/burndown`, so the issue list stays as fast as before.

## Why

A milestone page shows only a progress bar, so there is no way to tell whether a milestone is on track, when scope changed, or when it will finish. Acceptance criteria, in the order the issue lists them:

- **AC1** (chart with actual and ideal lines): the remaining and ideal lines. The axis runs from the first day to whichever is latest of today, the due date and the projection.
- **AC2** (history rebuilt from timeline events): each item's milestone, close, merge and reopen comments are replayed. Issues migrated in without those comments fall back to their row, and the replay always ends on the database's current state, so today's count matches the progress bar.
- **AC3** (scope additions and removals marked): ▲ and ▼ on the total line.
- **AC4** (projection shown only with enough data): hidden with under two days of history, when nothing has burned down over the window, when the work is done, or when the milestone is closed.
- **AC5** (hovering a day lists what changed): in the tooltip, and repeated with links under the chart.
- **AC6** (pull request toggle, off by default, in the URL): `include_pulls=1`; the checkbox reads it on load and writes it on change.
- **AC7** (edge cases): no due date hides the ideal line and says why; a changed due date uses the current one; an overdue milestone runs to today; a closed milestone ends on its close date (or on a later change, so the last point still matches the counters); an item added already closed widens the total but not the remaining count; an empty milestone shows a message instead of a chart.
- **AC8** (no access without permission, nothing private leaked): the endpoint sits in the same route group, with the same guards, as the milestone page. The milestone pages let in anyone who can read issues *or* pull requests, so the server counts and lists a kind only if the viewer can read it, and the checkbox is hidden from viewers who can't read pull requests.
- **AC9** (strings in `locale_en-US.json`): every visible string is under `repo.milestones.burndown.*`.
- **AC10** (unit tests for replay, toggle, ideal and projection): see below.

Deliberate differences from the issue's wording:
- The ideal line starts on the **first day with work**, not the creation day. Otherwise a milestone created empty and filled the next day draws a flat line at zero.
- A due date more than a year past the chart is not drawn. The test fixtures' year-9999 due date would otherwise flatten the chart.

## How it was tested

- **Go unit tests** (`models/issues/milestone_history_test.go`, `services/issue/milestone_burndown_test.go`):
  - The calculation is a pure function that takes `now` and a time zone, so 23 table cases cover every replay path: scope creep, items leaving, reopen, merge, an item added already closed, each fallback for missing history, the database winning when comments disagree, both closed-milestone endings, late, early and windowed projections, and the ideal line's limits.
  - Every case also asserts that the last point matches the items' current state.
  - Separate tests cover the per-day change lists, and dates across the New York daylight-saving changes.
  - The query tests check that only this milestone's and repository's history is read, that events come back in order, and that the batched lookups return every row.
- **Integration tests** (`tests/integration/milestone_burndown_test.go`):
  - `RealLifecycle` closes, reopens and moves issues through the real API and checks the history records Gitea actually wrote. The final counts alone can't show that, because the replay ends on the database's state either way.
  - `PullRequestsOnRequest` checks the toggle.
  - Two tests switch off the issues unit or the pull request unit and check that nothing of that kind is counted or listed. Both were confirmed to fail when the permission check is removed.
  - The rest check not-found and private-repository access.
- **Vitest** (`RepoMilestoneBurndown.utils.test.ts`): the summary sentence, ideal and projection lines, scope markers, axis range, tooltip lines, URL handling for the toggle (the issue list's filters survive it) and item links.
- **E2E** (`tests/e2e/milestone-burndown.test.ts`): the chart renders with its summary and accessible label; a closed issue appears in the change list with the right link; the toggle starts off, writes the URL, survives a reload and clears; the chart collapses and expands; an empty milestone shows its message.
- **Checked by hand,** because canvas drawing and multi-day history can't be produced through the API in real time: screenshots against a synthetic two-week history (markers, tooltip contents, step timing, the change list while moving the pointer to it), in light and dark themes, open and collapsed.

## CI / manual verification

Run locally on the branch after merging `main`:

- `go build ./...`, `go vet`, and golangci-lint v2.12.2 for Linux and for Windows (`gogit`) on the changed packages: 0 issues.
- `go test ./models/issues/ ./services/issue/`: pass under `TZ=UTC` and `TZ=America/New_York`.
- `go test -run 'Milestone|CloseReason' ./tests/integration/`: pass.
- `pnpm exec eslint`, `stylelint`, `vue-tsc`: clean. `pnpm exec vitest run`: 57 files, 307 tests pass.
- `GITEA_TEST_E2E_FLAGS='--project=chromium tests/e2e/milestone-burndown.test.ts tests/e2e/milestone.test.ts tests/e2e/repo-issues-chart.test.ts' make test-e2e`: 5 passed. Firefox e2e times out on this machine for existing tests too, so it was not used as a signal.
- `./.claude-students/check.sh`: ok (34 docs, guide 34/34).

## Design

See the Design Decision in #14: history is rebuilt from timeline comments when the chart is requested, rather than stored as daily snapshots. Later changes are listed under Why.

arjun-notes/proposed-issues.md:20:The warning color shipped in #3 marks issues and milestones due within 72 hours, but the state is carried entirely by text color — `tw-text-warning-text` for near due, `tw-text-red` for overdue — plus a hover tooltip. Everything else about the row is identical: the same `octicon-calendar`, the same date text. A user who cannot distinguish those hues from ordinary body text gets no signal at all. WCAG 2.1 §1.4.1 *Use of Color* (Level A) requires that color not be the only visual means of conveying information, and a hover tooltip does not satisfy it: it is unavailable on touch, requires the user to already suspect there is something to hover, and is useless when scanning thirty rows of an issue list. Contrast is *not* the problem here; `#9a6700` measures roughly 4.9:1 against white and already passes AA.

# Report: Sprint 1

**Team Name:** GiCoffee

**Team member names:** Vishav Chopra (vvchopra), Carson Rackley (CarsonRackley), Arjun Bhat (arjunsb26), Aman Bhoot (ab-wm), Jack Donohue (Jack-Donohue), Ethan Turner (controlled-opposition)

**Project Name:** Gitea

**Project Link:** [https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea)

## Sprint Overview

Brief narrative: what the team set out to do and what was actually delivered. Be honest about scope changes

### What we planned to do

At the start of the sprint, we were hit with the problem that most issues were ambitious and large in scope, making it difficult to cleanly assign work between different members of the team.

A number of large issues, namely #7, #12, #23 and #25, were cut down into smaller medium and small issues that were easier to manage. The plan was to complete these large issues, with members who split the issues into smaller issues working on the backbone of the problem, and then distributing the issues among other members to complete them.

### Scope Changes

While we certainly got close to completing all of the aforementioned large issues, and managed to complete all 13 issues in the Sprint 1 milestone (#12 through its sub-issues #53, #54 and #55, plus #50, #51, #61, #62, #63, #64, #14, #34 and #35), larger than expected issues and requests from product owners made it difficult to achieve our goal. The request from the product owner to complete #14, or “Add a burndown chart to milestones with an ideal line and projected finish,” was one of the main reasons we had to change the scope of this sprint.

Issue #14 was a large issue, and with one of our team members completely devoted to this purpose, we had to change the scope of the sprint to ensure we are able to complete the main issues, and leave cleanup work for the next sprint. Because of this, #64 was only picked up on the last day of the sprint (PR #81), the keyboard shortcut issues (#56, #57) were deferred and moved out of the milestone, and #52 was moved to Sprint 2.

Fortunately, however, we were able to complete #12 and #14 in full, along with the core of #7 and #25 (#50, #51 and #61–#64), so we still consider this sprint to be a success. The remaining sub-issues (#52, #65 and #56–#60) carry over into Sprint 2.

## Requirements & Design

Were specs complete before coding started? Any surprises? Key design decisions and brief rationale

### State of issues at the start of the sprint

Most of the issues carried over from Sprint 0 (#7, #12, #14, #23, #25, #34, #35) were written as summaries or proposals, not in the Sprint 1 spec format. Each owner rewrote their issue into a User Story, User Scenario, numbered Acceptance Criteria, Out of Scope and Open Questions, and a teammate posted a "Spec Reviewed" comment on the issue before implementation started.

Surprises:

- #35 was sent back ("Spec Reviewed: Not yet") for numbered acceptance criteria and was approved after it was revised.
- #14's spec was refined late, after implementation had already started.
- The review of #64 found that one of its acceptance criteria was already met by #62.
- Close reasons (#12) needed a database change and reached into automatic closes (commits, cross-references and the API), which became its own sub-issue (#55).

### Key decisions that led to the splitting of Issues

- **#7 Overhauled notifications system** → #50 (filter), #51 (bulk actions), #52 (sort). #52 was moved to Sprint 2 because it needs a database migration and a queue change.
- **#12 Close reasons** → #53 (storage and backend), #54 (UI), #55 (automatic and API closes). The issue was split by layer so that the backend could be merged first and the UI could build on it.
- **#25 Make dropdowns Accessible** → #61 (menu web component), #62 (menu migration), #63 (multi-select ARIA), #64 (icon-only triggers), #65 (Playwright regression suite). #61 had to be merged before #62 could use it.
- **#23 Keyboard navigation/shortcuts** → #56–#60, all deferred to keep the sprint scope achievable.
- **#14, #34 and #35** were kept as single issues. #14 is large and counts as two medium issues.

### Key design decisions

- **#50:** "Mark all as read" respects the active filter.
- **#51:** "Select all" only selects the notifications in the current view, with an explicit "Select all N notifications in this view" link. Bulk actions never reach outside the active view.
- **#53:** `CloseIssue` becomes a wrapper over a new `CloseIssueWithReason`, so existing callers keep working unchanged.
- **#54:** Picking "Duplicate" or "Other" opens a small popup under the close button, and each close reason gets its own icon.
- **#55:** Automatic closes record a default reason (completed for issues, not planned for pull requests).
- **#61:** The menu is built as a custom element under `web_src/js/webcomponents/`, without Fomantic.
- **#62:** Only static, server-rendered, single-select menus are migrated.
- **#63:** The existing Fomantic dropdown patch is extended rather than replaced.
- **#34:** `?due=` is parsed once into deadline bounds that both the database search and the issue indexer use.
- **#35:** A member or outside collaborator without two-factor authentication is treated as a non-member of the organization until they enrol. This is a reversible lockout: nothing is deleted.
- **#14:** Each milestone's history is rebuilt when the chart is requested, by replaying its items' timeline comments (milestone changes, closes, merges and reopens), and served from a separate JSON endpoint that the page loads after it renders, instead of a daily snapshot table that would have no history for existing milestones.

## Test Strategy

What kinds of tests were written? Were there changes you couldn't test automatically? Why?

Tests were written against the acceptance criteria, often one test per criterion:

- **Go unit tests** for models and services, run against the test database: #67, #68, #69, #70, #72, #73, #76, #77
- **Integration tests** that go through the full HTTP request path: #67, #68, #69, #70, #72, #73, #76, #77
- **Vitest** frontend unit tests: #68, #70, #71, #72, #75, #77, #81
- **Playwright end-to-end tests**: #68, #70, #71, #74, #75, #77, #81 (#71 also added a WebKit/Safari run)

In #67 and #68, the tests themselves were checked by deliberately breaking key lines of code and confirming that a test failed.

Changes we couldn't test automatically: screen reader behavior can't be driven in CI, so the accessibility work (#62/#74, #63/#75, #64/#81) asserts the ARIA attributes and live-region text instead. #81 also adds a development-mode warning for any dropdown trigger without an accessible name; the reviewer ran it on a local build, page by page, to find triggers the tests don't cover. Visual layout was checked by hand and with screenshots (#68, #74), and the Firefox end-to-end run only happens in CI.

## Risks and Retrospective

What worked:

- Splitting the large issues into sub-issues gave each member at least two medium issues and let work happen in parallel.
- The "Spec Reviewed" step caught gaps before coding started (#35 was revised before it was approved).
- Writing tests per acceptance criterion, and checking the tests by deliberately breaking code (#67, #68), produced well-specified PRs.
- CodeRabbit, added mid-sprint, gave quick first-pass reviews on #71–#77, alongside the required human rubric reviews.

What slowed the team:

- Review bottleneck: most PRs were opened in the last three days of the sprint (#71–#81, Oct 6–8), and one required approval with only a few active reviewers slowed merging. Four PRs (#73, #76, #77, #81) were merged in the final hours, and #81 was opened on the last evening.
- #77's burndown test passes on SQLite, MySQL and MSSQL but fails on PostgreSQL in CI, because events in the same second come back in a different order. It was merged on the last day with that check still failing, and the fix carries over into Sprint 2.
- #14 was a large issue that took one member the whole sprint, and its spec was refined late.
- Open PRs fell 25 commits behind `main` as other PRs merged and had to be updated.
- AI logs committed inside feature PRs made the diffs 8,000–36,000 added lines long, which made them harder to review.
- CodeRabbit's autofix pushed a commit directly to a teammate's branch (#76).
- Codebase size: Gitea has about 40 service packages, 85 module packages, and more than 300 migrations, so concept location still takes much longer than expected.

Changes for Sprint 2:

- Open PRs by the middle of the sprint and request a reviewer when opening them, aiming for a review within 24 hours.
- Don't start a branch until the spec is "Approved".
- Commit AI logs in a separate chore PR, as #78 did.
- Use CodeRabbit as a first pass only, with no autofix on someone else's branch without the author's OK.
- Update the branch from `main` before requesting a review.

_**User (2026-10-20 14:50:57Z)**_

what does the "include pull request" button do

---

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-20 14:51:04Z)**_

The **"Include pull requests"** checkbox decides whether the chart counts pull requests as well as issues.

- **Off (the default):** the chart counts only issues. In the demo, that's 8 issues at the start and 10 after Oct 13.
- **On:** pull requests in the milestone are counted as well. A merged PR counts as closed. In the demo, the one open PR raised the counts, added a second ▲ on Oct 11, and moved the projected finish from Nov 6 to Nov 19 (screenshot 4).
- **It's kept in the page URL.** Ticking it adds `?include_pulls=1`, so you can share the link and others see the same chart. It doesn't change the issue list's own filters under the chart.

Two rules apply depending on who's viewing:
- **The checkbox only shows if you can read both issues and pull requests.** Otherwise it's hidden.
- **Someone who can only read pull requests sees them by default.** Otherwise their chart would always say the milestone is empty; this was one of the bugs the review found.

It exists because Gitea's milestone progress bar already counts issues and PRs together. The #14 spec chose issues by default, since a burndown usually tracks the work items, with PRs available on request.

---

_**User (2026-10-20 14:56:40Z)**_

what exactly does the burndown chart accomplish

---

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-20 14:56:49Z)**_

The burndown chart shows whether a milestone will be finished by its due date, and why it's ahead or behind. Before it, a Gitea milestone page only had a progress bar and today's open/closed counts. That gives a snapshot but no history, no trend and no forecast.

It answers four questions:

1. **Are we on track?** The blue "remaining" line shows how many items were still open at the end of each day. The dashed "ideal" line goes straight from the first day of work down to zero on the due date. If blue is above the dashed line, you're behind; if it's below, you're ahead.

2. **When will we actually finish?** The red dotted line takes the recent pace (net items closed per day over the last 14 days) and extends it to zero. The summary turns that into a sentence, such as "Projected to finish on Nov 6, 12 days after the due date." If there isn't enough history to make a fair guess, it says so instead.

3. **Why did it slip?** A milestone often falls behind because work was added, not because the team was slow. The grey "total in milestone" line and the ▲/▼ markers show the days items were added or removed. In the demo, the ▲ on Oct 13 explains the jump back up.

4. **What happened on a given day?** Hover over a day and it lists the items that were closed, reopened, added or removed that day. The same list appears under the chart with links, so you can click through to each item.

This makes it useful at three points in a sprint:

- **During the sprint:** you can see early that you're slipping, while there's still time to cut scope or rebalance work.
- **At the end:** it's evidence for a retrospective. Your team's own Sprint 1 slipped because of scope (#14 itself), and this chart would have shown that.
- **When explaining to others:** a lead can show a product owner *why* the date moved ("two issues were added on day 3"), not just *that* it moved.

The history works for existing milestones from the start, with no setup needed. That's the design decision on your slide 2: the chart is rebuilt from each item's timeline (closes, reopens, milestone changes) instead of from a snapshot table that would only start recording once the feature shipped.

---

_**User (2026-10-20 14:57:36Z)**_

what does the y-axis provide

---

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-20 14:57:43Z)**_

The y-axis is a **count of items**: issues, plus pull requests if "Include pull requests" is ticked. Every item counts as exactly 1, because Gitea has no story points or weights. That was a deliberate out-of-scope decision in the #14 spec. A tiny typo fix and a big feature both count as 1.

All the lines share that axis, so each one reads as a number of items:

| Line | Y value means | Demo example |
|---|---|---|
| **Remaining** (blue) | Items still open at the end of that day | 5 on Oct 20 |
| **Total in milestone** (grey, dashed) | All items in the milestone, open or closed | 8, rising to 10 on Oct 13 |
| **Ideal** (black, dashed) | Where "remaining" should be to hit zero on the due date | 8 → 0 by Oct 25 |
| **Projected** (red, dotted) | Where "remaining" is heading at the current pace | 5 → 0 by Nov 6 |

The axis starts at 0, the finish line, and stretches to fit the largest value. That's why it tops out at 10 with issues only and at 15 once pull requests are included.

In a talk, the gap between the two dashed lines is the part worth pointing at:
- The vertical distance between **total** and **remaining** is the work already done.
- The distance between **remaining** and **ideal** is how far behind you are on a given day, counted in items.

_**User (2026-10-20 16:03:31Z)**_

expand on the 'out of scope' point

---

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-20 16:03:41Z)**_

The #14 spec lists five things the feature deliberately doesn't do. Here's each one, with the reason behind it.

1. **No `/api/v1` endpoint for burndown data.** The chart gets its data from a page endpoint (`/{owner}/{repo}/milestone/{id}/burndown`) that only serves the web page. A public API is a long-term promise to outside tools: it needs a fixed response format, swagger docs and versioning. That's a separate feature, and it can be added later on top of the same calculation.

2. **No story points or weights.** Gitea has no field for item size, so every item counts as 1. Adding points would mean a database change, a UI for entering them, and changes across issues and pull requests. That's a much bigger feature than the chart, so the y-axis counts items, not effort.

3. **No burndown on the milestones list or the user dashboard.** The chart is only on a single milestone's page. One chart per milestone on a list would mean one history calculation per milestone on every page load, which is too slow. It would also be a separate UI design job.

4. **No time zone per viewer.** Days are split in the server's time zone, the same zone Gitea stores due dates in. Everyone sees the same days, and the due date falls at the end of a chart day. Gitea doesn't store a time zone per user, so doing this per viewer would need a new user setting first.

5. **Issues moved to another repository lose their history.** History is read from the milestone's own repository, so a transferred issue drops out of every past day. A reviewer raised this (vvchopra, Jack). It was kept as a documented limitation because it's rare, and tracing history across repositories would make the query much more complex.

The spec also had open questions that were settled during the work, which are worth one line on a slide:
- **No due date:** the original spec said to hide the projection, but it's shown anyway because a finish date is useful without a deadline. Only the ideal line is hidden.
- **Far-off projections:** a projection more than a year out is stated in the summary but not drawn, so it can't squash the history into a sliver.

For the talk, one sentence covers it: "We drew the line at what the chart needs to be correct and fast: no new data model, no public API, no per-user settings. Each of those is a feature of its own."
